title: The estimate ignores the rounded PWM the strip receives, so the guarantee 'never above the supply' only holds in the model
body: `estimateAmps` and the budget use the continuous `Σ v²/255²`, but the Adalight output sends `LED_RESPONSE[v] = round(v²/255)`. Rounding adds up to 0.5/255 of a channel's current per channel, and the floor costs much more than modelled: v=12 encodes to PWM 1, which is 255 in v² units, not 144 (about 1.77x). I simulated real draw (Σ LED_RESPONSE after `applyPowerLimit`) for 173 WS2812B LEDs. It goes over the declared supply at 0.06 A (64 mA), 0.08 A, and 0.115-0.15 A, where floor=12 is chosen (e.g. 0.12 A -> 131 mA with 37 channels at 213 and the rest at 12). The table at 8 A is safe because of the 1.6 A margin, but the spec requirement and the randomized test only check the model, not what the LEDs draw. Estimate with `Σ LED_RESPONSE[v]` (an integer table lookup, still allocation-free), and check the floor with `LED_RESPONSE[12]` in the same units. Then confirm the √k + floor result against that estimate (e.g. a second pass, or a conservative factor).

title: Floor feasibility check uses 12² instead of the real cost of a channel at 12
body: `budget + ledCount * 3 * LIT_FLOOR * LIT_FLOOR <= supply` assumes a channel at 12 costs 12²/255² of a channel's current. The strip receives PWM 1/255, which is 0.078 mA per channel with WS2812B (about 41 mA for the 519 channels of the table, not 23). So the threshold where the floor is allowed (≈0.115 A) is too low: it should be around 0.2 A. Between those values the floor can push the real draw past the supply (see the other comment). Compute the floor cost as `ledCount * 3 * LED_RESPONSE[LIT_FLOOR] * 255` in v² units, or move the whole budget to PWM units.

title: The '23 mA, not 41' correction goes the wrong way
body: Decision 2 now bounds the floor at `mA_canal · (12/255)²` ≈ 0.044 mA per channel, or 23 mA on the table. The PR description calls this a correction of the earlier 41. But the LED draws in proportion to its PWM duty, which for 12 is `round(255·(12/255)²) = 1`, i.e. 20 mA/255 ≈ 0.078 mA per channel, or ~41 mA in total. The original figure was the physically correct one. The ≈0.115 A threshold on line 86 has the same problem. Fix the numbers together with the code.

title: Docs say the power limit uses LED_RESPONSE, but it never imports it
body: The stated reason for moving the gamma table to the core (decision 1, D108, the design goal that the gamma lives in one place, this comment, README §2.2 line 389, and the PR description) is that the power limit uses it to estimate. `power-limit.ts` does not import `LED_RESPONSE`: it re-encodes the curve as `v * v`. If the gamma changes, the encoder and the limit silently diverge. The real-draw gap in the other comments also comes from this duplication. Either make the limit read `LED_RESPONSE` (preferred), or reword the docs and D108 so they don't claim it does.

title: Seeded LCG loses precision and cycles after about 10k values
body: `state * 1103515245` reaches ~2.4e18, well past 2^53, so the low bits are lost and the sequence is no longer the intended LCG. With seed 135 it enters a cycle of about 10,466 values after ~5k draws. The randomized test draws about 1M values (519 per frame × 2100 frames), so most of its 'random' frames are reshuffled windows of the same short cycle. Use `Math.imul`-based 32-bit arithmetic (e.g. mulberry32 or xorshift32) so the property test really covers varied frames.

title: Property test checks the model, not the real output
body: The randomized test asserts `estimateAmps(frame) <= supplyAmps`, which uses the same `Σ v²` formula the limiter scales against. It is close to tautological, and it cannot catch the gap with the rounded PWM the strip receives. Also assert on the encoded draw (`Σ LED_RESPONSE[v] · mA_canal / 255`), so the test pins the physical guarantee the spec states.

title: Redundant `!limit` check and a duplicated limit computation
body: Once `output.type === 'adalight'`, `stripPowerLimit` always returns a limit, so `|| !limit` is dead (it is only there to satisfy the type checker). `main.ts` also builds every strip's limit once for the log and `startEngine` builds it again for the loop. It is pure, so the results match, but the log isn't describing the object the loop actually uses. Consider building the limits once in the composition root and passing them to both, or have `powerLimitMessage` take the `PowerLimit` directly.
